## Introduction

The objective of Project 2 is to work through importing, tidying and prepping messy data for downstream analysis using `tidyr` and `dplyr`. The following datasets have been chosen, stored as raw CSV files, and could be found in my Week 5 Assignment directory on [GitHub](https://github.com/shanicesmith98/data-607-assignments/tree/main/week-5-assignment):

- Motherboard / Vice's Car Thefts across the USA ([Discussion source](https://brightspace.cuny.edu/d2l/le/content/1344367/viewContent/41523045/View))

- Medical records ([Discussion source](https://brightspace.cuny.edu/d2l/le/content/1344367/viewContent/41523045/View))

- Highest Grossing Concert Tours by Women ([Discussion source](https://brightspace.cuny.edu/d2l/le/content/1344367/viewContent/41523045/View))

## Approach

As per the project requirements, each of the datasets will follow the same steps separately:

1.  Import the raw CSV files from the GitHub directory to preserve the original or scrapped structure. If possible, I will mark any blank records as NA, where needed.

2.  Read the csv file and inspect the structure of the files, then try to get the headers / columns to store as variables.

3.  Reshape the datasets from a wide format into a long format using `pivot_longer()` , which will collapse the columns into rows.

4.  Cleaning and tidying the datasets will happen next, to standardize variable names (casing, naming patterns, turning Y -\> Yes), convert column/row data types to the appropriate formats (ex. dates, numeric). I'll double check once more for any missing or NA records to make sure that's documented and accounted for prior to calculations.

5.  After, I can validate that the cleaned data is matching the unstructured data by verifying missing, duplicates or mislabeled variables are converted to the correct labeling.

6.  Lastly, I'll explore the cleaned and validated data by creating some graphs and charts with `ggplot2` for some simple analysis. Some questions I will have are how do Kia/Hyundai's share of total vehicle thefts change over time, how the clinical measurements compare across diagnosis groups, and adjusted vs actual gross for the tour.

```{r}
#| label: LoadingTidyVerse
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false

# helper and import chunk
library(tidyverse)

set.seed(1234)

theme_set(
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
    theme(axis.text = element_text(color = "grey20"),
          axis.title = element_text(color = "grey10"))
)

pct_label <- function(x) ifelse(is.na(x), "", paste0(round(x * 100), "%"))
```

## First Dataset — Kia/Hyundai thefts

**Challenges**

- For the car thefts, I anticipate the blank records being a challenge. The missing theft records from certain locations should not be counted as zeroes, but `NA`, which I can fix upon import of the file to avoid any complications - `na = c("", "N/A")`.

- Additionally, there are some inconsistencies of formatting of the locations, such as misspellings and the city/county pattern is not always enforced. Those will have to be fixed with a `case_when()` to catch before analysis.

### Loading in CSV

```{r}
#| label: LoadInCarThefts
car_thefts_raw_url <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/shanicesmith98/data-607-assignments/refs/heads/main/week-5-assignment/Motherboard_VICE_News_Kia_Hyundai_Theft_Dataset.csv"

car_theft_header_rows <- read_csv(car_thefts_raw_url, col_names = FALSE, n_max = 2,
                        col_types = cols(.default = "c"))

car_theft_data_body <- read_csv(car_thefts_raw_url, col_names = FALSE, skip = 2,
                       na = c("", "N/A"),
                       col_types = cols(.default = "c")) # skips double header rows

```

### Structure before tidying

```{r}
#| label: inspect-a
dim(car_theft_data_body) 
car_theft_header_rows[, 1:7]    # first two cities' worth of header
car_theft_data_body[, 1:7]      # first two cities' worth of data
```

We learn here that the data's structure is 45 data rows by 211 columns. Column 1 has the month and year from `Dec/19` through `Aug/23`. Row 1 is a merged city header (a name followed by two empty cells) and row 2 repeats `Kia/Hyundais`, `All`, `Percent` for each of 70 geographies. City and measure are values stored as column names, so 9,450 observations sit in 210 columns.

### Transformation

```{r}
#| label: rebuild-header-a

# Each city name appears once per three-column block, so two of every
# three header cells are empty and must be filled downward.
city_row    <- as.character(car_theft_header_rows[1, ])
measure_row <- as.character(car_theft_header_rows[2, ])

header_map <- tibble(
  position = seq_along(city_row),
  city     = str_trim(city_row),
  measure  = str_trim(measure_row)
) |>
  fill(city, .direction = "down")

n_distinct(header_map$city, na.rm = TRUE) # Output is 70 cities / column
count(header_map, measure) # 3 measures, 70 columns each

```

Trailing space is seen on several measure labels, which is why `str_trim()` is needed. Otherwise, later in the transformation process, two separate columns for `All` would be created instead of one.

```{r}
#| label: apply-names-a

# Combine city and measure into one name per column. "__" is used as the
# separator because no city name contains it, unlike "_", "," or " ".
new_names <- header_map |>
  mutate(col_name = if_else(position == 1,
                            "month",
                            str_c(city, measure, sep = "__"))) |>
  pull(col_name)

theft_named <- car_theft_data_body |> set_names(new_names)

names(theft_named)[1:7]
```

```{r}
#| label: pivot-a

theft_long <- theft_named |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols      = -month,
    names_to  = c("city", "measure"),
    names_sep = "__",
    values_to = "value"
  )

dim(theft_long)   # expect 9450 x 4

theft_tidy <- theft_long |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = measure, values_from = value) |>
  rename(
    kia_hyundai_thefts = `Kia/Hyundais`,
    all_thefts         = All,
    pct_reported       = Percent
  )

dim(theft_tidy)   # expect 3150 x 5
```

### Variable types and naming

```{r}
#| label: clean-a

theft_tidier <- theft_tidy |>
  mutate(
    # Turning source data format from "Dec/19" -> 2019-12-01
    month = parse_date(month, format = "%b/%y"),

    # Strip comma separators from numeric column: "1,014" -> 1014
    across(c(kia_hyundai_thefts, all_thefts), parse_number),

    # "8%" -> 8 -> 0.08, stored as a proportion for consistency
    pct_reported = parse_number(pct_reported) / 100,

    # Manually correcting typos and inconsistent formatting
    city = case_when(
      city == "Cincinatti"        ~ "Cincinnati",
      city == "Corpus Cristi, TX" ~ "Corpus Christi, TX",
      city == "Irving, Texas"     ~ "Irving, TX",
      TRUE ~ city
    )
  ) |>
  # Recompute the share rather than trusting the source column, which is
  # rounded to whole percents and blank for several reporting cities.
  mutate(
    pct_kia_hyundai = if_else(all_thefts > 0,
                              kia_hyundai_thefts / all_thefts,
                              NA_real_)
  )

glimpse(theft_tidier)
```

Column names are now using `snake_case` throughout with `kia_hyundai_thefts` and `all_thefts` count reported thefts per city-month.

### Missing-value decisions

```{r}
#| label: missingness-a

theft_tidier |>
  summarise(
    `City-months`      = n(),
    `Both counts`      = sum(!is.na(kia_hyundai_thefts) & !is.na(all_thefts)),
    `Kia count only`   = sum(!is.na(kia_hyundai_thefts) &  is.na(all_thefts)),
    `Total count only` = sum( is.na(kia_hyundai_thefts) & !is.na(all_thefts)),
    `Neither count`    = sum( is.na(kia_hyundai_thefts) &  is.na(all_thefts))
  )
```

Blank cells are kept as `NA` and not marked as zero. Some cities, such as Virginia Beach, Norfolk and Miami never report a total theft count; Frisco and Lincoln never report a Kia/Hyundai count; Atlanta, San Antonio and Henderson begin reporting only in January 2021. Treating those blanks as zeros would invent a denominator and hand me a fake 0% share. I'm not dropping the rows here either — the analysis below filters incomplete records only where they would break a calculation, so the counts above stay auditable.

### Analysis

I'm comparing each city's mean monthly Kia/Hyundai share before and after July 2022, the month the theft method got popular on social media. A city needs at least 12 months before and 6 after to qualify, so no mean rests on one or two observations. The statistic is the gap between those means in percentage points.

```{r}
#| label: analysis-a

share_change <- theft_tidier |>
  filter(!is.na(pct_kia_hyundai)) |>
  mutate(period = if_else(month < as.Date("2022-07-01"), "pre", "post")) |>
  group_by(city, period) |>
  summarise(months = n(), mean_share = mean(pct_kia_hyundai), .groups = "drop") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = period, values_from = c(months, mean_share)) |>
  filter(months_pre >= 12, months_post >= 6) |>
  mutate(change_pp = (mean_share_post - mean_share_pre) * 100) |>
  arrange(desc(change_pp))

nrow(share_change)   # cities meeting the coverage threshold
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-top-cities-a

share_change |>
  slice_max(change_pp, n = 10) |>
  transmute(
    City                       = city,
    `Share before (%)`         = round(mean_share_pre  * 100, 1),
    `Share Jul 2022 on (%)`    = round(mean_share_post * 100, 1),
    `Change (pct. points)`     = round(change_pp, 1),
    `Months (pre / post)`      = str_c(months_pre, " / ", months_post)
  )

top_cities <- share_change |> slice_max(change_pp, n = 6) |> pull(city)

```

```{r}
#| label: fig-theft-share-a
#| fig-cap: "Kia/Hyundai share of reported vehicle thefts in the six cities with the largest increase. The dashed line marks July 2022."
#| fig-alt: "Six small line charts, one per city, each rising sharply after mid-2022."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 5

theft_tidier |>
  filter(city %in% top_cities, !is.na(pct_kia_hyundai)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = month, y = pct_kia_hyundai)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = as.Date("2022-07-01"),
             linetype = "dashed", color = "grey60") +
  geom_line(color = "steelblue", linewidth = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~ city) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = pct_label) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "1 year", date_labels = "%Y") +
  labs(
    x = NULL,
    y = "Share of all vehicle thefts",
    caption = "Source: Motherboard / VICE News police-record dataset, Dec 2019 - Aug 2023"
  )
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-theft-share-data
#| tbl-cap: "Monthly Kia/Hyundai share of reported vehicle thefts (%) for the six cities in Figure 1. Blank cells are months the agency did not report."

theft_tidier |>
  filter(city %in% top_cities) |>
  mutate(Month = format(month, "%b %Y"),
         share_pct = round(pct_kia_hyundai * 100, 1)) |>
  select(Month, month, city, share_pct) |>
  arrange(month) |>
  select(-month) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = city, values_from = share_pct)

```

### Conclusions

The tidy dataset holds `r nrow(theft_tidier)` city-months, `r sum(!is.na(theft_tidier$pct_kia_hyundai))` of them with both counts reported, which leaves `r nrow(share_change)` cities with enough coverage to compare periods. The biggest jump is `r share_change$city[1]`, going from `r round(share_change$mean_share_pre[1] * 100, 1)`% to `r round(share_change$mean_share_post[1] * 100, 1)`% — a gain of `r round(share_change$change_pp[1], 1)` percentage points — and the median change across qualifying cities is `r round(median(share_change$change_pp), 1)` points. @fig-theft-share-a shows that rise is sudden rather than gradual, landing mostly in late 2022 and holding through August 2023. That fits a vulnerability being exploited once it was widely known, not a slow change in what cars are on the road. The main limit is coverage: `r sum(is.na(theft_tidier$pct_kia_hyundai))` city-months are missing a count, so this describes reporting agencies rather than all 70 locations.

## Second Dataset — Medical records

**Challenges**

- Like the first dataset, I also anticipate the blank records being a challenge here with the medical records. The missing records from certain locations should not be counted as zeroes, but `NA`, which I can fix upon import of the file to avoid any complications - `na = c("", "nan", "N/A")`.

- Certain variables, such as Smoker, has inconsistent labeling and will need to be reformatted to one standardized pattern.

### Data source

```{r}
#| label: import-b

medical_records_raw_url <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/shanicesmith98/data-607-assignments/refs/heads/main/week-5-assignment/realworld_medical_dirty_dataset.csv"

# NA values have to be addressed here to avoid issues with 'nan' being turned into a catergory
medical_records_raw_data <- read_csv(
  medical_records_raw_url,
  na = c("", "nan", "N/A"),
  col_types = cols(
    Patient_ID     = col_character(),
    Age            = col_double(),
    Gender         = col_character(),
    Blood_Pressure = col_double(),
    Cholesterol    = col_double(),
    BMI            = col_double(),
    Smoker         = col_character(),
    Diagnosis      = col_character(),
    Admission_Date = col_date(format = "%Y-%m-%d"),
    Notes          = col_character()
  )
)
```

### Inspecting structure

```{r}
#| label: inspect-b

dim(medical_records_raw_data)
names(medical_records_raw_data)
head(medical_records_raw_data, 5)
sum(duplicated(medical_records_raw_data$Patient_ID))   # Output: 0
```

The raw file is 100 rows by 10 columns, one row per patient, with IDs `P1000` through `P1099` and no duplicates. Four of the columns (`Age`, `Blood_Pressure`, `Cholesterol`, `BMI`) are four separate measurements of the same patient, column names are inconsistently cased, and the categorical columns carry several spellings of the same value.

```{r}
#| label: inspect-b-categories

count(medical_records_raw_data, Gender)
count(medical_records_raw_data, Smoker)
count(medical_records_raw_data, Diagnosis)
count(medical_records_raw_data, Notes)
```

`Gender` holds five spellings of two values (`Male`, `MALE`, `male`, `Female`, `FEMALE`). `Smoker` mixes `Yes`/`Y` and `No`/`N`. `Admission_Date` is the one column needing no treatment: valid ISO-8601 throughout.

### Transformation steps

### Consistent variable names

```{r}
#| label: rename-b

# Using snake_case throughout
med <- medical_records_raw_data |>
  rename(
    patient_id     = Patient_ID,
    age_years      = Age,
    gender         = Gender,
    blood_pressure = Blood_Pressure,
    cholesterol    = Cholesterol,
    bmi            = BMI,
    smoker_raw     = Smoker,
    diagnosis      = Diagnosis,
    admission_date = Admission_Date,
    notes          = Notes
  )
```

### Standardizing inconsistent values

```{r}
#| label: recode-b

med <- med |>
  mutate(
    # Five spellings collapse to two with one title-case call.
    gender = str_to_title(gender),

    # Yes/Y and No/N become a logical, which makes later proportions trivial.
    is_smoker = case_when(
      smoker_raw %in% c("Yes", "Y") ~ TRUE,
      smoker_raw %in% c("No",  "N") ~ FALSE,
      TRUE ~ NA
    ),

    # Diagnosis has BOTH a "None" level and missing values; these mean different things and are kept separate.
    # "None" = could mean examined, nothing found. NA = not recorded.
    diagnosis_group = if_else(is.na(diagnosis), "Not recorded", diagnosis)
  ) |>
  select(-smoker_raw)   # drop the raw column now that is_smoker exists

count(med, gender)
count(med, is_smoker)
count(med, diagnosis_group)
```

### Reshaping the measurements to long form

```{r}
#| label: pivot-b

med_tidy <- med |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols      = c(age_years, blood_pressure, cholesterol, bmi),
    names_to  = "measure",
    values_to = "value"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    unit = case_when(
      measure == "age_years"      ~ "years",
      measure == "blood_pressure" ~ "mmHg",
      measure == "cholesterol"    ~ "mg/dL",
      measure == "bmi"            ~ "kg/m2"
    ),
    measure_label = case_when(
      measure == "age_years"      ~ "Age",
      measure == "blood_pressure" ~ "Blood pressure",
      measure == "cholesterol"    ~ "Cholesterol",
      measure == "bmi"            ~ "BMI"
    ),
    facet_label = str_c(measure_label, " (", unit, ")")
  )

dim(med_tidy)   # Output: 400 x 12
```

The id columns — `patient_id`, `gender`, `is_smoker`, `diagnosis`, `admission_date`, `notes` — are left untouched by the pivot because they describe the *patient*, not the measurement. Only the four measured quantities move. The result is 100 patients × 4 measurements = 400 rows, which is the grain that lets one `group_by()` answer a question about all four measurements at once.

### Missing-value decisions

```{r}
#| label: tbl-missingness-b

med_tidy |>
  group_by(Measurement = facet_label) |>
  summarise(
    Patients   = n(),
    Reported   = sum(!is.na(value)),
    Missing    = sum(is.na(value)),
    `% missing` = round(100 * mean(is.na(value)), 1),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

No row and no patient is dropped. Every summary below uses `na.rm = TRUE` and reports the number of patients behind each statistic in its own column.

### Analysis

We're doing two comparisons on the long data. First, mean and median of each measurement by diagnosis group — I'm showing both because the measurements are pre-binned, and the median is the more honest summary of a discrete variable. Second, mean measurement for smokers against non-smokers. Counts go with every figure and nothing is imputed.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-by-diagnosis-b
#| tbl-cap: "Mean and median of each clinical measurement by diagnosis group, with the number of patients reporting each measurement. These are the values plotted in Figure 2."

med_summary <- med_tidy |>
  group_by(Measurement = facet_label, Diagnosis = diagnosis_group) |>
  summarise(
    Patients = sum(!is.na(value)),
    Mean     = round(mean(value,   na.rm = TRUE), 1),
    Median   = round(median(value, na.rm = TRUE), 1),
    .groups  = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(Measurement, Diagnosis)

med_summary
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-by-smoker-b

smoker_summary <- med_tidy |>
  filter(!is.na(is_smoker), !is.na(value)) |>
  group_by(Measurement = facet_label, is_smoker) |>
  summarise(n = n(), mean_value = mean(value), .groups = "drop") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = is_smoker, values_from = c(n, mean_value)) |>
  transmute(
    Measurement,
    `Smokers (n)`      = n_TRUE,
    `Smokers mean`     = round(mean_value_TRUE,  1),
    `Non-smokers (n)`  = n_FALSE,
    `Non-smokers mean` = round(mean_value_FALSE, 1),
    Difference         = round(mean_value_TRUE - mean_value_FALSE, 1)
  )

smoker_summary
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-measures-by-diagnosis-b
#| fig-cap: "Mean value of each clinical measurement by diagnosis group, labelled with the number of patients reporting that measurement."
#| fig-alt: "Four panels of bar charts comparing mean measurement values across four diagnosis groups."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 6

med_summary |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Diagnosis, y = Mean)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue", width = 0.7) +
  geom_text(aes(label = str_c("n=", Patients)), vjust = -0.4, size = 3) +
  facet_wrap(~ Measurement, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))) +
  labs(
    x = NULL,
    y = "Mean value",
    caption = "Synthetic teaching dataset; 100 patients, admissions during 2023"
  ) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 20, hjust = 1))
```

### Conclusions

The tidy dataset holds `r nrow(med_tidy)` patient-measurement rows, `r sum(!is.na(med_tidy$value))` with a reported value and `r sum(is.na(med_tidy$value))` missing. Differences between diagnosis groups are small: mean age spans only `r min(med_summary$Mean[med_summary$Measurement == "Age (years)"])` to `r max(med_summary$Mean[med_summary$Measurement == "Age (years)"])` years, and mean blood pressure under 6 mmHg. @fig-measures-by-diagnosis-b shows why — every measurement takes just five distinct values, so the data is pre-binned and any real difference gets squashed toward the bin width. That rules out correlation or regression on these columns, which is why I stopped at group means and medians. I also kept `None` (`r sum(med$diagnosis == "None", na.rm = TRUE)` patients, examined with nothing found) separate from unrecorded (`r sum(is.na(med$diagnosis))` patients), since merging them would overstate how many patients I know are healthy.

## Third Dataset — Highest Grossing Concert Tours by Women

**Challenges**

- Rank 7 shows up twice (Celine Dion, Pink) and rank 8 is missing, so I can't trust `Rank` as an identifier and will rank the tours myself.

- The format for the numeric variables will need to be stripped to be solely numbers by removing the dollar signs and commas for more reliable calculations.

### Import Data

```{r}
#| label: import-c

high_grossing_women_tours_raw_url <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/shanicesmith98/data-607-assignments/refs/heads/main/week-5-assignment/tours_dataset.csv"

# Everything reads as text: currency columns carry "$" and thousands
# separators, and several numeric cells end in a footnote marker.
tours_raw_data <- read_csv(high_grossing_women_tours_raw_url, col_types = cols(.default = "c"))
```

### Structure before tidying

```{r}
#| label: inspect-c

dim(tours_raw_data)
names(tours_raw_data)
head(tours_raw_data, 5)
```

Twenty rows by 11 columns, one row per tour. Four problems are visible in the head: currency stored as text (`"$780,000,000"`), footnote markers inside otherwise numeric cells (`"2[5]"`, `"$229,100,000[b]"`), status symbols inside the tour title (`"The Eras Tour †"`), and a year *range* in a single column (`"2023–2024"`) that holds two variables.

```{r}
#| label: inspect-c-names

# The two currency column names contain a non-breaking space (U+00A0),
# not a regular space. They look identical on screen, so a rename()
# matching "Actual gross" fails silently.
str_detect(names(tours_raw_data), "\u00a0")
```

A fifth problem is not visible at all: `Rank` is not unique. Rank 7 appears twice and rank 8 is absent, so the column cannot serve as a key.

### Transformation steps

### Repairing the column names

```{r}
#| label: fix-names-c

# Replace non-breaking spaces with ordinary ones before renaming anything.
names(tours_raw_data) <- names(tours_raw_data) |>
  str_replace_all("\u00a0", " ") |>
  str_trim()

tours <- tours_raw_data |>
  rename(
    source_rank    = Rank,
    peak           = Peak,
    all_time_peak  = `All Time Peak`,
    actual_gross   = `Actual gross`,
    adjusted_gross = `Adjusted gross (in 2022 dollars)`,
    artist         = Artist,
    tour_title     = `Tour title`,
    years          = `Year(s)`,
    shows          = Shows,
    average_gross  = `Average gross`,
    source_ref     = `Ref.`
  )
```

### Capturing the footnote markers before deleting them

```{r}
#| label: flags-c

# The dagger marks tours still running when the table was compiled, which
# means their grosses are partial. That is real information, so it is
# captured as a column BEFORE the symbol is stripped out.
tours <- tours |>
  mutate(
    is_ongoing   = str_detect(tour_title, "\u2020"),   # †
    has_marker   = str_detect(tour_title, "[\u2021*]") # ‡ and *
  )

sum(tours$is_ongoing)   # expect 2
sum(tours$has_marker)   # expect 3
```

The source page's legend is not part of the CSV, so the meaning of `‡` and `*` cannot be recovered from this file. They are recorded in `has_marker` and flagged as an open question rather than guessed at; the two `†` tours are treated as incomplete throughout.

### Converting text to numbers

```{r}
#| label: parse-c

# Remove bracketed footnote references like [4], [a], [21].
strip_notes <- function(x) str_remove_all(x, "\\[[0-9a-z]+\\]")

tours <- tours |>
  mutate(
    # Titles: drop footnotes AND status symbols, then trim the leftover space
    tour_title = tour_title |>
      strip_notes() |>
      str_remove_all("[\u2020\u2021*]") |>
      str_trim(),

    # Peaks: footnotes removed first, then integer conversion
    across(c(peak, all_time_peak), ~ as.integer(strip_notes(.x))),

    # Currency: footnotes first, then parse_number() strips "$" and commas
    across(c(actual_gross, adjusted_gross, average_gross),
           ~ parse_number(strip_notes(.x))),

    across(c(source_rank, shows), as.integer)
  )
```

### Splitting the year range

```{r}
#| label: years-c

tours <- tours |>
  separate_wider_delim(
    years,
    delim   = "\u2013",                        # EN-DASH, not a hyphen
    names   = c("year_start", "year_end"),
    too_few = "align_start"                    # single-year tours get NA
  ) |>
  mutate(
    across(c(year_start, year_end), as.integer),
    year_end = coalesce(year_end, year_start), # a one-year tour ends the year it starts
    tour_years = year_end - year_start + 1
  )
```

### Reshaping the two gross figures to long form

```{r}
#| label: pivot-c

tours_tidy <- tours |>
  # average_gross is derived (actual_gross / shows) and is recomputed below;
  # source_ref is a citation artifact belonging in Sources, not in the data.
  select(-average_gross, -source_ref) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols      = c(actual_gross, adjusted_gross),
    names_to  = "gross_basis",
    values_to = "gross_usd"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    gross_basis = if_else(gross_basis == "actual_gross",
                          "Nominal (as earned)",
                          "Adjusted to 2022 USD")
  )

dim(tours_tidy)   # expect 40 x 13
```

Nominal and inflation-adjusted dollars are the same quantity measured on two bases. Side by side in separate columns they invite direct comparison of figures that are not comparable; stacked, the basis becomes an explicit grouping variable and every chart and table must declare which one it uses.

### Why the derived column is recomputed

```{r}
#| label: check-derived-c

tours |>
  mutate(
    recomputed = actual_gross / shows,
    difference = round(average_gross - recomputed, 0)
  ) |>
  filter(abs(difference) > 1) |>
  select(tour_title, shows, actual_gross, average_gross, recomputed, difference)
```

I'm comparing the two gross bases by ranking every tour twice, once on nominal and once on adjusted gross, then taking the difference. That difference shows how much inflation adjustment moves the standings. Revenue per show is recomputed as `actual_gross / shows` and reported only for the 18 completed tours, since the two ongoing ones have partial grosses against partial show counts.

### Analysis

The analysis compares the two gross bases. Each tour is ranked twice — once by nominal gross and once by inflation-adjusted gross — and the difference between those ranks measures how much inflation adjustment changes the standings. Revenue per show is recomputed as `actual_gross / shows` and reported separately for the 18 completed tours, since the two ongoing tours have partial grosses against a partial show count.

```{r}
#| label: analysis-c

rank_shift <- tours |>
  mutate(
    rank_nominal  = rank(-actual_gross,   ties.method = "min"),
    rank_adjusted = rank(-adjusted_gross, ties.method = "min"),
    rank_change   = rank_nominal - rank_adjusted   # positive = climbs
  ) |>
  arrange(rank_adjusted)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-rank-shift-c

rank_shift |>
  filter(abs(rank_change) >= 2) |>
  transmute(
    Artist                  = artist,
    Tour                    = tour_title,
    Years                   = str_c(year_start, "-", year_end),
    `Nominal rank`          = rank_nominal,
    `Adjusted rank`         = rank_adjusted,
    `Places moved`          = rank_change
  )
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-per-show-c

tours |>
  filter(!is_ongoing) |>
  mutate(gross_per_show = actual_gross / shows) |>
  slice_max(gross_per_show, n = 8) |>
  transmute(
    Artist              = artist,
    Tour                = tour_title,
    Shows               = shows,
    `Actual gross ($M)` = round(actual_gross / 1e6, 1),
    `Per show ($M)`     = round(gross_per_show / 1e6, 2)
  )
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-gross-basis-c
#| fig-cap: "Nominal versus inflation-adjusted gross for each tour, ordered by adjusted gross. Daggered tours were still running when the source table was compiled."
#| fig-alt: "Dumbbell chart of 20 tours, each with two points connected by a line."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 8

# Order the y-axis by adjusted gross so the chart reads as a ranking
title_order <- tours |> arrange(adjusted_gross) |> pull(tour_title)

tours_tidy |>
  mutate(tour_title = factor(tour_title, levels = title_order)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = gross_usd / 1e6, y = tour_title)) +
  geom_line(aes(group = tour_title), color = "grey75", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(aes(color = gross_basis, shape = gross_basis), size = 2.6) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = function(x) paste0("$", x, "M")) +
  labs(
    x       = "Tour gross",
    y       = NULL,
    color   = "Basis",
    caption = "Source: Wikipedia ranking of highest-grossing female solo tours, compiled from Billboard Boxscore"
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-gross-basis-data
#| tbl-cap: "Nominal and inflation-adjusted gross for each tour in millions of US dollars, ordered by adjusted gross. These are the values plotted in Figure 3."

tours |>
  arrange(desc(adjusted_gross)) |>
  transmute(
    Artist                = artist,
    Tour                  = tour_title,
    `Nominal gross ($M)`  = round(actual_gross   / 1e6, 1),
    `Adjusted gross ($M)` = round(adjusted_gross / 1e6, 1),
    `Difference ($M)`     = round((adjusted_gross - actual_gross) / 1e6, 1)
  )
```

### Conclusions

The tidy dataset holds `r nrow(tours_tidy)` rows, `r nrow(tours)` tours on two gross bases. Nominal grosses total \$`r round(sum(tours$actual_gross) / 1e9, 2)` billion against \$`r round(sum(tours$adjusted_gross) / 1e9, 2)` billion adjusted to 2022 dollars, and that gap sits almost entirely in the older tours. @fig-gross-basis-c shows the two bases pulling apart with age: recent tours are nearly a single point, while mid-2000s tours show a wide spread. Cher's *Living Proof: The Farewell Tour* climbs from `r rank_shift$rank_nominal[rank_shift$tour_title == "Living Proof: The Farewell Tour"]` to `r rank_shift$rank_adjusted[rank_shift$tour_title == "Living Proof: The Farewell Tour"]` once adjusted. Pink's *Summer Carnival* drops from `r rank_shift$rank_nominal[rank_shift$tour_title == "Summer Carnival"]` to `r rank_shift$rank_adjusted[rank_shift$tour_title == "Summer Carnival"]`, not because it earned less, but because it has no inflation behind it. Revenue per show splits two business models: the Eras Tour made about \$13.9M per show over 56 shows, Cher's run \$0.6M over 325, and both land near the top. The limits are that `source_rank` isn't unique, `all_time_peak` is missing for `r sum(is.na(tours$all_time_peak))` of `r nrow(tours)` tours, and `r sum(tours$is_ongoing)` tours were still running, so I left them out of the per-show table.
